params.question: Which of the following symptoms is best explained by forward failure in heart failure?

answers.text: Orthopnoea

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Orthopnoea is a backward failure symptom. Lying flat shifts fluid from the legs into the pulmonary circulation, worsening congestion behind the failing left ventricle.

answers.text: Ankle oedema

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Ankle oedema is a right-sided backward failure symptom caused by elevated systemic venous pressure, not by reduced cardiac output reaching the tissues.

answers.text: Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: PND is a left-sided backward failure symptom. Fluid gradually redistributes to the lungs after lying down, causing the patient to wake gasping 1–2 hours after falling asleep.

answers.text: Fatigue and reduced exercise tolerance

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Forward failure means inadequate cardiac output reaching the tissues. Skeletal muscles receive less blood, causing fatigue; the kidneys respond by increasing nocturnal urine output (nocturia).

overallFeedback.feedback: Forward failure means reduced cardiac output to the body, causing fatigue and nocturia. Backward failure means blood backing up behind the failing ventricle — left-sided causes breathlessness and pulmonary congestion, right-sided causes oedema and venous distension.

Correct! Fatigue and reduced exercise tolerance result from inadequate cardiac output reaching the tissues — this is forward failure. Backward failure symptoms (breathlessness, oedema) come from blood backing up behind the failing ventricle.

interactions.label: In diastolic heart failure, the ejection fraction is reduced because the ventric

params.question: In diastolic heart failure, the ejection fraction is reduced because the ventricle cannot generate adequate contractile force.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is false. In diastolic heart failure the ventricle contracts normally — ejection fraction is preserved (≥50%). The problem is impaired relaxation and filling due to a stiff, hypertrophied ventricle. Reduced ejection fraction occurs in systolic dysfunction, where the ventricle is dilated and contracts weakly.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct! In diastolic dysfunction the ventricle contracts normally and ejection fraction is preserved (≥50%). The problem is a stiff, thick-walled ventricle that fails to relax and fill properly during diastole. Reduced ejection fraction characterises systolic dysfunction, where the dilated ventricle contracts weakly.

interactions.label: A patient with heart failure has an ECG showing an irregularly irregular rhythm

params.question: A patient with heart failure has an ECG showing an irregularly irregular rhythm with no identifiable P waves. Why is this particular finding especially significant in a heart failure patient?

answers.text: It confirms the diagnosis of heart failure on its own

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The ECG alone cannot confirm heart failure. A truly normal ECG makes heart failure less likely, but atrial fibrillation indicates a rhythm disturbance, not a definitive heart failure diagnosis.

answers.text: It indicates two conditions reinforcing each other, since this arrhythmia both causes and worsens heart failure

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Atrial fibrillation and heart failure have a bidirectional relationship: AF worsens HF through loss of atrial contraction and rapid ventricular rate, while HF promotes AF through atrial dilatation and fibrosis. Every patient with both needs a CHA₂DS₂-VASc score to guide anticoagulation.

answers.text: It proves the heart failure is caused by ischaemic heart disease

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Ischaemic aetiology on ECG is suggested by pathological Q waves (prior infarction) or ST-segment changes, not by atrial fibrillation. AF has multiple causes beyond coronary artery disease.

answers.text: It means the patient requires immediate cardiac resynchronisation therapy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: CRT is indicated for left bundle branch block (widened QRS with broad notched R waves in lateral leads) combined with reduced ejection fraction, not for atrial fibrillation. These are distinct ECG patterns with different management pathways.

overallFeedback.feedback: Atrial fibrillation (irregularly irregular rhythm, absent P waves) and heart failure reinforce each other: AF worsens HF through loss of atrial contraction and rapid rate, while HF predisposes to AF through atrial dilatation. This is why every patient with both needs a CHA₂DS₂-VASc score for anticoagulation assessment.

Correct! AF and heart failure form a vicious cycle: AF reduces cardiac output through loss of atrial kick and rapid rate, while HF promotes AF through atrial stretch. Recognising this bidirectional relationship — and assessing stroke risk with CHA₂DS₂-VASc — is essential.

interactions.label: A stable outpatient with HFrEF (ejection fraction 30%) is on enalapril, carvedil

params.question: A stable outpatient with HFrEF (ejection fraction 30%) is on enalapril, carvedilol, and spironolactone. Her symptoms are controlled with furosemide. Which additional drug class should be added to complete guideline-directed medical therapy?

answers.text: Digoxin

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Digoxin can reduce symptoms and heart failure hospitalisations, but it does not improve survival. It is not one of the four pillars of guideline-directed medical therapy for HFrEF.

answers.text: Higher-dose loop diuretics

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Loop diuretics relieve congestion and improve symptoms but do not reduce mortality. This patient is already on furosemide for symptom control; increasing the dose does not add a disease-modifying benefit.

answers.text: SGLT2 inhibitors (e.g., dapagliflozin or empagliflozin)

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: SGLT2 inhibitors are the fourth pillar of GDMT. They reduce cardiovascular death and HF hospitalisations irrespective of diabetes status. With ACEi, beta-blocker, and MRA already prescribed, adding an SGLT2i completes all four pillars.

answers.text: Calcium channel blockers

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (verapamil, diltiazem) are generally avoided in HFrEF due to their negative inotropic effects. They are not among the four pillars of heart failure therapy.

overallFeedback.feedback: The four mortality-reducing pillars in HFrEF are: (1) ACEi/ARB/ARNI, (2) beta-blockers (carvedilol, metoprolol succinate, bisoprolol), (3) mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (spironolactone), and (4) SGLT2 inhibitors (empagliflozin, dapagliflozin). Diuretics and digoxin control symptoms but lack proven survival benefit.

Correct! The four pillars of HFrEF therapy are: (1) ACEi/ARB/ARNI, (2) evidence-based beta-blockers, (3) mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, and (4) SGLT2 inhibitors. Diuretics and digoxin improve symptoms but do not extend survival.

interactions.label: A 35-year-old woman with known rheumatic mitral stenosis presents with six weeks

params.question: A 35-year-old woman with known rheumatic mitral stenosis presents with six weeks of low-grade fever, weight loss, fatigue, and night sweats. Blood cultures grow Streptococcus viridans. Which form of infective endocarditis does this presentation represent?

answers.text: Acute infective endocarditis caused by Staphylococcus aureus

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Acute IE develops over days, presents with high spiking fever, rigors, and rapid valve destruction, and is typically caused by S. aureus on a previously normal valve. This patient's six-week indolent course is characteristic of subacute disease.

answers.text: Subacute infective endocarditis on a pre-damaged rheumatic valve

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Classic subacute IE: indolent six-week course, low-grade constitutional symptoms, Streptococcus viridans (oral flora entering the blood), and underlying rheumatic valve disease providing damaged endothelium where less virulent organisms can adhere and form vegetations.

answers.text: Acute right-sided endocarditis from intravenous drug use

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Right-sided (tricuspid) endocarditis in IV drug users typically presents acutely with S. aureus, high fever, and septic pulmonary emboli. This patient has left-sided rheumatic valve disease and a subacute course with viridans streptococcus.

answers.text: Culture-negative endocarditis requiring empirical therapy alone

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Blood cultures have identified Streptococcus viridans, making this culture-positive endocarditis. Directed antibiotic therapy can be selected based on the organism's sensitivity pattern.

overallFeedback.feedback: This is subacute infective endocarditis. Key features: indolent course (weeks to months), low-grade symptoms, less virulent organisms (classically Streptococcus viridans from oral flora), and pre-existing valve damage — in India, most commonly rheumatic. Acute IE, by contrast, develops over days with high fever and S. aureus.

Correct! This is textbook subacute IE: an indolent course over weeks, constitutional symptoms, viridans streptococcus from oral flora, and rheumatic valve disease — in India, the most common predisposing condition — providing the damaged surface for bacterial colonisation.

interactions.label: A young adult presents with a continuous 'machinery' murmur in the left infracla

params.question: A young adult presents with a continuous 'machinery' murmur in the left infraclavicular area, bounding pulses, and no cyanosis. Which congenital heart lesion is most likely, and why is the patient acyanotic?

answers.text: Tetralogy of Fallot — blood shunts left to right across the VSD

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Tetralogy of Fallot is a cyanotic lesion. Blood shunts right to left (not left to right) because of right ventricular outflow tract obstruction, sending deoxygenated blood into the systemic circulation.

answers.text: Atrial septal defect — the shunt is too small to cause cyanosis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: ASD produces fixed splitting of the second heart sound, not a continuous murmur. ASD is acyanotic because of its left-to-right shunt direction, not because the shunt is small.

answers.text: Patent ductus arteriosus — the shunt is left to right, so only oxygenated blood recirculates

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: PDA produces a continuous machinery murmur because the aorta-to-pulmonary artery pressure gradient persists throughout systole and diastole. The left-to-right shunt recirculates oxygenated blood through the lungs — no deoxygenated blood enters the systemic circulation, so there is no cyanosis.

answers.text: Transposition of the great arteries — two parallel circuits are mixing adequately

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: TGA produces cyanosis from birth because the systemic and pulmonary circuits run in parallel without adequate mixing. It does not produce a machinery murmur and requires urgent intervention in the neonatal period.

overallFeedback.feedback: The continuous machinery murmur is characteristic of patent ductus arteriosus. It is acyanotic because blood flows left to right (aorta to pulmonary artery), recirculating oxygenated blood. Cyanotic lesions have right-to-left shunts, allowing deoxygenated blood into the systemic circulation.

Correct! The continuous machinery murmur is characteristic of PDA, where the aorta-to-pulmonary artery gradient never reverses. The left-to-right shunt recirculates oxygenated blood, keeping the patient pink — the defining feature of acyanotic congenital heart disease.
